account:
It is eight o'clock on day 1, and I am at town hall for office hours. I have read and returned my appointment book. Today includes the ten o'clock mill inspection, council letters after lunch, tea at the dockside cottage, and an eighteen hundred great hall lighting inspection recorded in a separate addendum.

Something unusual seems to be happening around that evening inspection. Yesterday freight had commissioned two hundred loaves, personally giving the baker twenty-four emeralds and seventy-two wheat. The secretary reported a further five hundred twenty-eight wheat needed, with mill stock and delivery terms still uncertain. Yet this morning the baker says all two hundred jubilee loaves are ready, and he and freight are delivering them to the four great hall table chests. I have not seen those loaves myself or learned how the remaining grain was obtained.

The baker, innkeeper, and secretary were gathered at town hall unusually early. The innkeeper repeatedly asked me to attend the eighteen hundred lighting inspection, although it was already booked with the builder. He directed the bread storage and mentioned discussing the account privately afterward. When I asked whose jubilee this was, he did not identify one; instead, he said he commissioned the bread for an inn hospitality arrangement and would settle the baker's account himself. I have explicitly authorized no treasury payment.

My suspicion is that the lighting inspection may also be an occasion for some kind of celebration or hospitality gathering, perhaps a surprise they do not want to explain to me yet. Two hundred jubilee loaves are rather more than a lighting inspection needs. That is only an inference: I do not know whose jubilee is intended, who will attend, or whether there is any concealed purpose at all. The innkeeper appears to be organizing, the baker and freight supplying bread, and the builder involved with the lighting. The secretary maintains the appointments and has investigated the grain supply, but I have no evidence that the secretary knows more about a celebration. For now I intend to keep my appointments, learn what I can at the mill, and attend the hall inspection without treating this private bread order as a town expense.
